EC2 Instances Deep: EC2 provides virtual machines. Instance families: general (t3, m6i), compute (c6i), memory (r6i, x2gd), storage (i3, d2), GPU (p4, g5). Purchase options: On-Demand (pay per hour/sec), Reserved (1-3yr, up to 72% off), Spot (up to 90% off, interruptible), Dedicated Host. User data runs at boot. Placement groups control instance placement for low latency or HA.

# Launch EC2
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --instance-type t3.medium \
  --key-name my-key \
  --security-group-ids sg-xxx \
  --subnet-id subnet-xxx \
  --user-data file://bootstrap.sh \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=ec2-s3-role \
  --block-device-mappings "DeviceName=/dev/xvda,Ebs={VolumeSize=50,VolumeType=gp3}"

# Spot instance
aws ec2 request-spot-instances \
  --spot-price "0.05" \
  --instance-count 2 \
  --launch-specification file://spot-spec.json
EC2 Networking & Security Groups: Security Groups are stateful firewalls attached to ENIs. Rules: allow only (no deny), evaluate all rules. NACLs are stateless firewalls at subnet level (allow/deny, rule numbers). Elastic IPs are static public IPs. ENIs are virtual network cards. VPC Flow Logs capture traffic metadata.

# Create security group
aws ec2 create-security-group \
  --group-name web-sg \
  --description "Web server SG" \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxx

# Add rules
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-xxx \
  --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-xxx \
  --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 10.0.0.0/8

# Allocate Elastic IP
aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc
aws ec2 associate-address --instance-id i-xxx --allocation-id eipalloc-xxx
EC2 Auto Scaling: Auto Scaling maintains desired instance count. Launch template specifies instance config. Scaling policies: target tracking (e.g., keep CPU at 50%), step scaling, scheduled scaling. Health checks replace unhealthy instances. Cooldown periods prevent rapid scaling. Lifecycle hooks run custom actions during scale events.

# Create launch template
aws ec2 create-launch-template \
  --launch-template-name web-template \
  --launch-template-data file://template.json

# Create Auto Scaling group
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=web-template \
  --min-size 2 --max-size 10 --desired-capacity 2 \
  --vpc-zone-identifier "subnet-xxx,subnet-yyy" \
  --target-group-arns arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...

# Target tracking policy
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --policy-name cpu-target \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration file://cpu-target.json
Elastic Load Balancing: ALB (Application LB): HTTP/HTTPS, path-based routing, host-based routing, WebSockets. NLB (Network LB): TCP/UDP/TLS, ultra-low latency, static IP. Gateway LB: transparent inspection of traffic. Target groups route to instances, IPs, or Lambda. Sticky sessions via cookies. Health checks detect failures. Cross-zone load balancing distributes evenly.

# Create ALB
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer \
  --name my-alb \
  --subnets subnet-xxx subnet-yyy \
  --security-groups sg-xxx \
  --scheme internet-facing

# Create target group
aws elbv2 create-target-group \
  --name web-tg \
  --protocol HTTP --port 80 \
  --vpc-id vpc-xxx \
  --health-check-path /health

# Add target
aws elbv2 register-targets \
  --target-group-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:... \
  --targets Id=i-xxx Id=i-yyy

# Create listener
aws elbv2 create-listener \
  --load-balancer-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:... \
  --protocol HTTPS --port 443 \
  --certificates CertificateArn=arn:aws:acm:... \
  --default-actions Type=Forward,TargetGroupArn=arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...
AWS Lambda: Lambda runs code without servers. Runtimes: Node.js, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, custom (provided.al2). Triggers: API Gateway, S3, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge, Kinesis. Max execution 15 min, max memory 10GB, max ephemeral storage 10GB. Concurrency limit per account (1000 default). Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity. Provisioned concurrency keeps instances warm. Lambda@Edge runs at CloudFront edge locations.

# Create Lambda function
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name my-function \
  --runtime python3.12 \
  --role arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/lambda-role \
  --handler index.handler \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip \
  --memory-size 512 \
  --timeout 30

# Add S3 trigger
aws lambda create-event-source-mapping \
  --function-name my-function \
  --event-source-arn arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket \
  --events s3:ObjectCreated:*

# Python function code
# import json
# def handler(event, context):
#     return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps({'message': 'Hello!'})}
ECS, EKS & Fargate: ECS runs Docker containers at scale. Launch types: Fargate (serverless, no EC2 to manage) and EC2 (control over instances). EKS is managed Kubernetes. ECR stores container images. Task definitions describe containers (CPU, memory, ports, env vars). Services maintain desired task count with load balancer integration.

# ECS task definition
{ "family": "web-app",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "app",
    "image": "nginx:alpine",
    "memory": 512,
    "cpu": 256,
    "portMappings": [{"containerPort": 80, "protocol": "tcp"}],
    "environment": [{"name": "NODE_ENV", "value": "production"}]
  }],
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "cpu": "256",
  "memory": "512"
}

# Create ECS service
aws ecs create-service \
  --cluster my-cluster \
  --service-name web-service \
  --task-definition web-app:1 \
  --launch-type FARGATE \
  --desired-count 3 \
  --network-configuration "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[subnet-xxx],securityGroups=[sg-xxx]}"
Elastic Beanstalk: Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS — upload code, AWS handles provisioning, load balancing, auto scaling, monitoring. Platforms: Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, PHP, Ruby, Go, Docker. Environments: Web tier (ALB + ASG) and Worker tier (SQS + background jobs). Customize with .ebextensions config files. Easy for MVPs and standard web apps.

# Initialize EB project
pip install awsebcli
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
eb init -p node.js-20 my-app --region us-east-1

# Create environment
eb create production --cname my-app-prod

# Deploy
eb deploy

# Open in browser
eb open

# .ebextensions/options.config
option_settings:
  aws:autoscaling:asg:
    MinSize: '2'
    MaxSize: '6'
  aws:elasticbeanstalk:environment:
    EnvironmentType: LoadBalanced
  aws:autoscaling:launchconfiguration:
    InstanceType: t3.small
EC2 Image Builder & AMIs: EC2 Image Builder automates AMI creation. Pipeline steps: source image, build components (install packages), test components (validate), distribute to regions. Golden AMIs ensure consistent instances. Systems Manager Parameter Store tracks latest AMI IDs. Automate AMI refresh in Auto Scaling via lifecycle hooks.

# Create Image Builder pipeline
# Console or SDK — configures:
# - Source: Amazon Linux 2023
# - Build component: Install packages, harden
# - Test component: Run security scans
# - Distribute: us-east-1, eu-west-1

# Systems Manager parameter for AMI
aws ssm put-parameter \
  --name /ami/web-app \
  --value ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --type String

# AMI cleanup lifecycle
autoscaler:
  - Create new AMI via Image Builder
  - Update SSM parameter
  - Launch new instance via ASG instance refresh

S3 Deep Dive: Amazon S3 is object storage with 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability. Storage classes: Standard (frequent access), Intelligent-Tiering (auto-cost optimization), Standard-IA (infrequent), One Zone-IA (lower cost, single AZ), Glacier Instant (archival, ms retrieval), Glacier Flexible (min retrieval), Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, 12hr retrieval). Versioning protects against deletes. Lifecycle policies transition between classes. S3 Event Notifications trigger Lambda/SQS/SNS.

# Create bucket
aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket --region us-east-1

# Enable versioning
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# Lifecycle policy
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

# lifecycle.json: transition to IA after 30d, Glacier after 90d, expire after 365d
{
  "Rules": [{
    "Id": "archive-rule",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": { "Prefix": "" },
    "Transitions": [
      { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
      { "Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
    ],
    "Expiration": { "Days": 365 }
  }]
}

# Pre-signed URL (temporary access)
aws s3 presign s3://my-bucket/private.txt --expires-in 3600
S3 Security & Encryption: S3 security: Block Public Access (account/bucket level). Bucket policies (resource-based). IAM policies (identity-based). ACLs (legacy). Encryption: SSE-S3 (AES-256, AWS managed), SSE-KMS (KMS keys, audit trail), SSE-C (customer provided key), client-side encryption. Object Lock (WORM — write once read many). S3 Access Points simplify managing access for large datasets.

# Block public access
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

# Bucket policy (allow CloudFront only)
{ "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::cloudfront:user/CloudFront Origin Access Identity E1A2B3C4D5E6" },
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"
  }]
}

# Enable default encryption
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption \
  --bucket my-bucket \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}'
EBS & Instance Storage: EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides persistent block storage for EC2. Volume types: gp3 (baseline 3000 IOPS, 125 MB/s, max 16000 IOPS), io2 (provisioned IOPS, 99.999% durability), st1 (throughput optimized, HDD), sc1 (cold HDD). Snapshots are incremental backups to S3. EBS Multi-attach for clustered workloads. EBS Fast Snapshot Restore for instant snapshot hydration. Instance Store is ephemeral (data lost on stop/terminate).

# Create EBS volume
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --volume-type gp3 \
  --size 100 \
  --iops 5000 \
  --throughput 250 \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a

# Attach to EC2
aws ec2 attach-volume \
  --volume-id vol-xxx \
  --instance-id i-xxx \
  --device /dev/xvdf

# Create snapshot
aws ec2 create-snapshot \
  --volume-id vol-xxx \
  --description "Pre-upgrade backup"

# Enable Fast Snapshot Restore
aws ec2 enable-fast-snapshot-restores \
  --availability-zones us-east-1a us-east-1b \
  --source-snapshot-id snap-xxx
EFS & FSx: EFS is managed NFS for Linux. Elastic — grows/shrinks automatically. Performance modes: General Purpose (default, latency-sensitive) and Max I/O (high-throughput, parallel). Throughput modes: Bursting and Provisioned. Lifecycle management moves files to EFS IA after N days. EFS Replication for cross-region DR. FSx for Windows File Server (SMB, AD integration) and FSx for Lustre (high-performance, HPC/AI).

# Create EFS
aws efs create-file-system \
  --performance-mode generalPurpose \
  --throughput-mode bursting \
  --creation-token my-efs

# Create mount target (one per AZ)
aws efs create-mount-target \
  --file-system-id fs-xxx \
  --subnet-id subnet-xxx \
  --security-groups sg-xxx

# Mount on EC2
sudo mount -t nfs4 -o nfsvers=4.1,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,hard,timeo=600,retrans=2,noresvport fs-xxx.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/ /mnt/efs

# FSx for Lustre (HPC)
# aws fsx create-file-system --file-system-type LUSTRE --storage-capacity 1200 --subnet-ids subnet-xxx
CloudFront CDN: CloudFront is a global CDN with 400+ edge locations. Origins: S3, ALB, EC2, Lambda Function URL, HTTP server. Behaviors route by path pattern. Price classes: All, 200 (most), NA+EU only. SSL/TLS termination via ACM. Geo-restriction (whitelist/blacklist countries). Lambda@Edge for custom logic. OAC (Origin Access Control) secures S3 origins. Real-time logs to Kinesis. WAF integration for DDoS protection.

VPC Design: VPC is your isolated network in AWS. CIDR block defines IP range (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16). Subnets divide the VPC (public for internet-facing, private for internal). Route tables direct traffic. Internet Gateway (IGW) for public internet access. NAT Gateway for private subnets to reach internet (outbound only). VPC Peering connects VPCs within or across accounts. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs and on-prem. Endpoints (Gateway: S3/DynamoDB; Interface: other services) provide private access without IGW.

# Create VPC
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.2.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1b

# Internet Gateway
aws ec2 create-internet-gateway
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id vpc-xxx --internet-gateway-id igw-xxx

# NAT Gateway
aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc
aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id subnet-xxx --allocation-id eipalloc-xxx

# VPC Peering
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id vpc-xxx --peer-vpc-id vpc-yyy

# VPC Endpoint (Gateway type)
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-xxx --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-xxx
Route53 DNS: Route53 is a DNS service (authoritative + resolver). Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (verify), Alias (Route53-specific, maps to AWS resources — free, works at zone apex). Routing policies: Simple, Weighted, Latency, Failover, Geolocation, Geoproximity, Multi-value. Health checks monitor endpoint health and route away from failures. Private hosted zones for internal DNS. DNSSEC for security.
AWS WAF & Shield: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that protects HTTP endpoints. Rule groups: IP set, SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting, geo-match, regex patterns. Managed rule groups from AWS (Core, SQL DB, Admin Protection, Known Bad Inputs). Shield Standard is free, protects against DDoS (L3/L4). Shield Advanced ($3k/mo) adds L7 DDoS protection, cost protection, DRT (DDoS Response Team). WAF integrates with CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync.

# Create WAF IP set
aws wafv2 create-ip-set \
  --name allowed-ips \
  --scope CLOUDFRONT \
  --ip-address-version IPV4 \
  --addresses '["203.0.113.0/24", "198.51.100.0/24"]'

# Create WAF ACL
aws wafv2 create-web-acl \
  --name web-acl \
  --scope CLOUDFRONT \
  --default-action Allow={} \
  --rules file://waf-rules.json \
  --visibility-config SampledRequestsEnabled=true,CloudWatchMetricsEnabled=true,MetricName=web-acl-metric

# Associate with CloudFront
# aws wafv2 associate-web-acl --web-acl-arn arn:aws:wafv2:... --resource-arn arn:aws:cloudfront::...distribution/xxx
AWS KMS & Secrets Manager: KMS manages encryption keys. Customer managed keys vs AWS managed keys. Automatic annual key rotation. Envelope encryption: generate a data key to encrypt data, encrypt the data key with a KMS key. Key policies control who can use/administer keys. Grant allows temporary access. Secrets Manager stores secrets (DB passwords, API keys) with automatic rotation via Lambda. Parameter Store (free) stores config data and secrets.

# Create KMS key
aws kms create-key --description "My app encryption key"
aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/my-app-key --target-key-id xxx

# Encrypt with KMS
aws kms encrypt \
  --key-id alias/my-app-key \
  --plaintext fileb://secret.txt \
  --output text --query CiphertextBlob | base64 --decode > encrypted.txt

# Secrets Manager
aws secretsmanager create-secret \
  --name prod/db/password \
  --secret-string '{"username":"admin","password":"P@ssw0rd"}'

# Get secret
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db/password

# Parameter Store
aws ssm put-parameter --name /app/db-url --value "postgresql://..." --type String --tier Standard

AWS Account & Root User: Create an AWS account at aws.amazon.com. Root user has full unrestricted access — enable MFA immediately. Never use root for daily tasks. Create IAM users and roles instead. Set up billing alerts. Use AWS Organizations to manage multiple accounts centrally. Enable CloudTrail in all regions.

# AWS CLI setup
aws configure
# Access Key ID / Secret Access Key / Region / Output

# Check caller identity
aws sts get-caller-identity

# List available regions
aws ec2 describe-regions

# Enable CloudTrail
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name my-trail --s3-bucket-name my-logs
aws cloudtrail start-logging --name my-trail
IAM Users, Groups & Roles: IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls access. Users are individuals. Groups organize users with shared permissions. Roles are assumed by services (EC2, Lambda) or federated users. Policies are JSON documents with Allow/Deny effects. Follow least privilege. Use managed policies when possible.

# Create IAM user
aws iam create-user --user-name devops
aws iam create-access-key --user-name devops

# Add user to group
aws iam create-group --group-name admins
aws iam add-user-to-group --user-name devops --group-name admins

# Attach managed policy
aws iam attach-group-policy \
  --group-name admins \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess

# Create IAM role for EC2
aws iam create-role --role-name ec2-s3-role --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json
IAM Policies Deep: IAM policies have: Version (2012-10-17), Statement list with Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (service:operation), Resource (ARN), and optional Condition (IP, time, MFA, tags). Use policy variables ${aws:username}. Managed policies vs inline. Permission boundaries limit max permissions. Service Control Policies (SCP) in Organizations.
AWS Organizations & SCPs: AWS Organizations centrally manages multiple accounts. Root OU contains all accounts. Create OUs for structure (Production, Staging, Sandbox). Service Control Policies (SCPs) restrict max permissions across accounts. Consolidate billing for volume discounts. Use AWS SSO for user access across accounts.
Regions, AZs & Edge Locations: AWS has 30+ regions worldwide (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1, etc.). Each region has 3-6 Availability Zones (AZs) — isolated data centers. Edge Locations are CDN endpoints (400+). Use multiple AZs for HA. Choose region based on latency, compliance, cost, and service availability. Some services are global (IAM, Route53, CloudFront).

# List AZs for a region
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region us-east-1

# Check service availability per region
# aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /aws/service/global-infrastructure/regions

# Recommended regions
# us-east-1: N. Virginia (most services, lowest cost)
# eu-west-1: Ireland (EU presence)
# ap-southeast-1: Singapore (Asia)
# sa-east-1: Sao Paulo (South America)

RDS Deep Dive: RDS manages relational databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora. Multi-AZ: synchronous standby replica in another AZ for HA (failover is automatic). Read replicas: async replication for read scaling (up to 15). Automated backups with point-in-time recovery (up to 35 days). Manual snapshots persist beyond retention. Enhanced Monitoring (CloudWatch metrics per second). Performance Insights for query analysis. RDS Proxy for connection pooling.

# Create RDS PostgreSQL
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --engine postgres \
  --engine-version 16.3 \
  --db-instance-identifier mydb \
  --db-instance-class db.m6g.large \
  --allocated-storage 200 \
  --storage-type gp3 \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password secret \
  --multi-az \
  --backup-retention-period 35 \
  --enable-performance-insights \
  --enable-cloudwatch-logs-exports '["postgresql"]'

# Create read replica
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier mydb-ro \
  --source-db-instance-identifier mydb \
  --region us-west-2
Aurora: Amazon Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible with cloud-native architecture. 6-way replication across 3 AZs — only 1/6 of data written (quorum). Auto-scaling storage from 10GB to 128TB. Aurora Serverless v2 scales to 0 ACUs (pay per second). Global Database: 1 primary region, up to 5 secondary regions with <1s replication. Backtrack: rewind DB to a specific time without restore. Parallel Query pushes analytics to storage layer.

# Create Aurora cluster
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --engine-version 16.4 \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-pg \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password secret

# Add writer instance
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier aurora-pg-writer \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large \
  --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-pg

# Serverless v2
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --engine aurora-postgresql \
  --serverless-v2-scaling-configuration MinCapacity=0.5,MaxCapacity=128 \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-serverless

# Backtrack (MySQL Aurora only)
aws rds backtrack-db-cluster \
  --db-cluster-identifier aurora-mysql \
  --backtrack-to "2025-12-01T00:00:00Z"
DynamoDB: DynamoDB is fully managed NoSQL key-value/document DB. Single-digit ms latency at any scale. Primary key: partition key (HASH) or composite (HASH + RANGE). Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request, auto-scales) and Provisioned (RCU/WCU, auto-scaling). DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is in-memory cache for microsecond reads. Global Tables are multi-region, multi-writer (active-active). Streams capture changes for Lambda triggers or Kinesis. TTL auto-expires items.

# Create table
aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name Users \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S AttributeName=email,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=email,KeyType=RANGE \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

# Put item
aws dynamodb put-item \
  --table-name Users \
  --item '{ "id": {"S": "user1"}, "name": {"S": "Alice"}, "age": {"N": "30"} }'

# Query (must use partition key)
aws dynamodb query \
  --table-name Users \
  --key-condition-expression "id = :id" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{ ":id": {"S": "user1"} }'

# Enable TTL
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live \
  --table-name Sessions \
  --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=expiresAt
ElastiCache & MemoryDB: ElastiCache provides managed Redis and Memcached. Redis: multi-AZ, replication, persistence, pub/sub, sorted sets, streams, Lua scripting. Memcached: simple, multi-threaded, no persistence. Cluster Mode shards data across nodes (up to 500 shards). Global Datastore for cross-region replication. MemoryDB is Redis-compatible, durable (write-ahead log), for microservices requiring both speed and durability. Use cases: session store, caching, rate limiting, leaderboards, message queues.

# Create Redis cluster
aws elasticache create-cache-cluster \
  --cache-cluster-id redis-cluster \
  --cache-node-type cache.r6g.large \
  --engine redis \
  --num-cache-nodes 1 \
  --multi-az-enabled \
  --automatic-failover-enabled

# Create Redis with cluster mode
aws elasticache create-replication-group \
  --replication-group-id redis-sharded \
  --replication-group-description "Sharded Redis" \
  --cache-node-type cache.r6g.large \
  --engine redis \
  --num-node-groups 3 \
  --replicas-per-node-group 1

# Connect via redis-cli
# redis-cli -h my-cluster.xxxxx.clustercfg.use1.cache.amazonaws.com -p 6379
Redshift & Data Analytics: Redshift is cloud data warehouse (petabyte-scale). Columnar storage, massively parallel (MPP). Node types: DC (dense compute), DS/RA3 (managed storage). Distribution styles: KEY, ALL, EVEN. Sort keys define data order per block. Redshift Spectrum queries data directly in S3 without loading. Automatic workload management (WLM) prioritizes queries. Concurrency Scaling handles burst queries. Materialized views for pre-computed aggregates. Unload data to S3 for analysis.

# Create Redshift cluster
aws redshift create-cluster \
  --cluster-identifier dw-cluster \
  --node-type dc2.large \
  --number-of-nodes 4 \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password secret

# Unload to S3
UNLOAD ('SELECT region, SUM(sales) FROM sales GROUP BY region')
TO 's3://my-bucket/unload/'
IAM_ROLE 'arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/redshift-s3'
PARQUET
PARTITION BY (region);

# External table (Spectrum)
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE spectrum.sales (
  id INT, amount DECIMAL, region VARCHAR(50)
)
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.io.parquet.serde.ParquetHiveSerDe'
LOCATION 's3://my-bucket/sales-parquet/';

CloudFormation: CloudFormation is IaC (Infrastructure as Code) on AWS. Templates written in YAML/JSON. Resources define AWS components. Parameters allow customization at deploy time. Outputs export values for cross-stack references. Change sets preview changes before applying. Nested stacks compose complex infrastructure. Drift detection checks if real-world resources match the template. StackSets deploy across accounts/regions via Organizations. DeletionPolicy controls resource retention on stack delete.

# Template structure
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Web application infrastructure
Parameters:
  EnvName:
    Type: String
    Default: production

CI/CD with CodePipeline: CodePipeline automates build-test-deploy. Source: CodeCommit, GitHub, Bitbucket, S3. Build: CodeBuild (managed build server, pay per minute). Deploy: CodeDeploy (EC2, Lambda, ECS), Elastic Beanstalk, CloudFormation. Stages run sequentially with manual approval gates. Artifacts stored in S3. CloudWatch Events trigger pipelines on source changes.

CloudWatch Monitoring: CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and alarms. Metrics: CPU, memory, disk, network, custom metrics. Alarms: threshold-based, composite (multiple conditions), anomaly detection. Logs: agent collects from EC2, streams to log groups. Logs Insights queries logs with SQL-like syntax. Contributor Insights analyzes top contributors (IPs, endpoints). Synthetics (Canaries) monitor endpoints with Node.js scripts. ServiceLens traces requests across services (X-Ray integration). Dashboards visualize metrics in one place.

# Put custom metric
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \
  --metric-name ActiveUsers \
  --namespace MyApp \
  --value 42 \
  --unit Count

# Create alarm
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name HighCPU \
  --alarm-description "CPU > 80% for 5 min" \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Average \
  --period 300 \
  --threshold 80 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 2 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:ops-topic

EventBridge & Step Functions: EventBridge is a serverless event bus. Sources: AWS services, SaaS (Datadog, Zendesk), custom apps. Rules filter events and route to targets (Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions). Pipes connects sources to targets with filtering and enrichment. Step Functions orchestrates distributed workflows (visual state machine). Standard Workflows (up to 1-year duration) vs Express (up to 5-min, high volume). States: Task, Choice, Parallel, Map, Wait, Succeed, Fail. Error handling with retries and catch.
AWS Budgets & Cost Control: AWS Budgets track spending and send alerts. Types: Cost budget, Usage budget, Savings Plans budget, Reservation budget. Budget actions can apply IAM policy or stop EC2 instances when threshold is exceeded. Cost Explorer visualizes spend. Compute Optimizer recommends right-sizing. Savings Plans (Compute, EC2 Instance, SageMaker) offer discounts for commitment. Trusted Advisor checks cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits. Consolidated billing aggregates usage across accounts.

VPC Deep Dive: VPC is the foundation of AWS networking. Subnets (public/private) segment IP ranges. Route tables direct traffic to IGW (public) or NATGW (private). NAT Gateway enables outbound internet for private subnets — costs ~$0.045/hr + data processed. VPC Peering connects VPCs directly (no transitive peering). Security Groups (stateful, allow-only) vs NACLs (stateless, allow/deny, rule numbers). Common mistake: forgetting NACL rules are stateless — must configure both inbound and outbound rules separately. VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata for analysis. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs/on-prem via a hub. Use VPC endpoints for private access to S3/DynamoDB without NAT/IGW.

# Create VPC with public/private subnets
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.2.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a

# Internet Gateway
aws ec2 create-internet-gateway
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id vpc-xxx --internet-gateway-id igw-xxx

# NAT Gateway (costs money! ~$0.045/hr + data)
aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc
aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id subnet-public --allocation-id eipalloc-xxx

# Route tables
aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id vpc-xxx
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-xxx --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id igw-xxx
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id rtb-xxx --subnet-id subnet-public

# Security Group (stateful — return traffic allowed automatically)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-xxx --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# NACL (stateless — need both inbound AND outbound rules)
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id acl-xxx --ingress --rule-number 100 --protocol tcp --port-range From=443,To=443 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id acl-xxx --egress --rule-number 100 --protocol tcp --port-range From=1024,To=65535 --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow

# VPC Peering
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id vpc-main --peer-vpc-id vpc-peer
aws ec2 accept-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-xxx
Route53 & DNS: Route53 is AWS's DNS service. Hosted zones contain DNS records for a domain. Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (cannot be used at zone apex), MX (mail), TXT (verification), Alias (Route53-specific, maps to AWS resources, works at zone apex, free). Routing policies: Simple (single record), Weighted (A/B testing), Latency (best performance), Failover (active-passive DR), Geolocation (by user location), Geoproximity (by resource location). Health checks monitor endpoints. Common mistake: using CNAME at zone apex — use Alias instead. Enable DNSSEC for DNS spoofing protection.
CloudFront & CDN: CloudFront is AWS's global CDN with 400+ edge locations. Distributions define content delivery configuration. Origins: S3 buckets, ALBs, EC2, custom HTTP servers. Behaviors route by URL path pattern. Lambda@Edge executes code at edge locations (viewer/origin request/response) — use for A/B testing, URL rewrites, authentication. Price classes: Price Class All (all edges), Price Class 200 (most, cheaper), Price Class 100 (US+Europe, cheapest). Invalidations clear edge caches (charged per path). OAC (Origin Access Control) secures S3 origins. WAF integration for DDoS. Common mistake: caching sensitive data — set appropriate Cache-Control and Cookie/QueryString forwarding policies.
DynamoDB: DynamoDB is serverless NoSQL with single-digit ms latency. Tables contain items (up to 400KB each). Primary key: Partition Key (HASH) alone or Composite (HASH + RANGE/Sort Key). GSIs (Global Secondary Indexes) have different partition/sort keys — eventually consistent, add after table creation. LSIs (Local Secondary Indexes) same partition key, different sort key — created only at table creation, strongly consistent. DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is an in-memory cache for microsecond reads. Capacity modes: On-Demand (pay per request, best for variable traffic) and Provisioned (RCU/WCU, cheaper for predictable traffic). Streams capture changes for 24h. TTL auto-expires items. Common mistake: scanning instead of querying — always Query with a partition key.

# Create table with GSI
aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name Orders \
  --attribute-definitions \
    AttributeName=CustomerId,AttributeType=S \
    AttributeName=OrderDate,AttributeType=S \
    AttributeName=Status,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema \
    AttributeName=CustomerId,KeyType=HASH \
    AttributeName=OrderDate,KeyType=RANGE \
  --global-secondary-indexes '[
    {
      "IndexName": "StatusIndex",
      "KeySchema": [{"AttributeName": "Status", "KeyType": "HASH"}, {"AttributeName": "OrderDate", "KeyType": "RANGE"}],
      "Projection": {"ProjectionType": "ALL"}
    }
  ]' \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

# Query (efficient — uses partition key)
aws dynamodb query --table-name Orders \
  --key-condition-expression "CustomerId = :cid AND OrderDate BETWEEN :start AND :end" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":cid": {"S": "cust-123"}, ":start": {"S": "2025-01-01"}, ":end": {"S": "2025-12-31"}}'

# Scan (expensive — avoid in production!)
aws dynamodb scan --table-name Orders --filter-expression "Status = :s"

# DAX (cache for microsecond reads)
aws dynamodb create-cluster --cluster-name my-dax --node-type dax.r5.large --replication-factor 3 --iam-role-arn arn:aws:iam::xxx:role/dax-role

# Enable TTL
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name Sessions --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=ttl
SQS & SNS: SQS is fully managed message queuing. Standard queues: unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO queues: exactly-once processing, first-in-first-out, 3000 msg/s max (with batching). Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) capture messages that fail after maxReceiveCount retries. Visibility timeout hides messages during processing — set longer than your processing time. Long polling reduces empty responses and costs. SNS is pub/sub messaging. Topics fan out messages to subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS). Fan-out pattern: SNS sends to multiple SQS queues for parallel processing. Message filtering with filter policies. Common mistake: forgetting to delete messages from SQS after processing (they reappear after visibility timeout!).

# Create standard queue
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name my-queue --attributes '{
  "VisibilityTimeout": "30",
  "MessageRetentionPeriod": "345600",
  "ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds": "20"
}'

# Create DLQ and set redrive policy
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name my-queue-dlq
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/xxx/my-queue \
  --attributes '{
    "RedrivePolicy": "{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:xxx:my-queue-dlq\",\"maxReceiveCount\":\"3\"}"
  }'

# Send and receive
aws sqs send-message --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/xxx/my-queue --message-body "Hello"
aws sqs receive-message --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/xxx/my-queue
aws sqs delete-message --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/xxx/my-queue --receipt-handler xxx

# FIFO queue (exactly-once, ordered)
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name my-queue.fifo --attributes '{"FifoQueue": "true", "ContentBasedDeduplication": "true"}'

# SNS topic
aws sns create-topic --name my-topic

# Subscribe SQS to SNS (fan-out)
aws sns subscribe --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:my-topic --protocol sqs \
  --notification-endpoint arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:xxx:my-queue

# Publish message
aws sns publish --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:my-topic --message "Hello"

# Filter policy (receive only specific event types)
# Subscription attribute: {"event": ["order_created", "order_shipped"]}
Step Functions & Workflows: Step Functions orchestrates distributed workflows as state machines. Standard Workflows: up to 1-year duration, exactly-once execution, billed per state transition. Express Workflows: up to 5-min duration, at-least-once, billed by execution time/memory. State types: Task (invoke Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, SQS), Choice (if/else), Parallel (fan-out), Map (iterate array), Wait (delay), Succeed/Fail (terminate). Error handling: Retry (exponential backoff, maxAttempts) and Catch (redirect to fallback state). Timeouts prevent stuck executions. Heartbeats for long-running tasks. Common mistake: not setting appropriate timeouts — workflows can hang indefinitely.
CloudWatch & Monitoring: CloudWatch is the single source of truth for AWS observability. Metrics: AWS service metrics (CPU, requests, latency) and custom metrics (up to 15-second granularity). Alarms: threshold-based, anomaly detection (ML-based), composite alarms (combine multiple conditions). Alarm actions trigger SNS, Auto Scaling, EC2 stop/reboot. Logs Insights queries logs with a SQL-like query language. Contributor Insights analyzes top contributors. Synthetics Canaries monitor endpoints. Dashboards combine metrics, logs, and alarms. Common mistake: not setting dimension combinations on custom metrics (each unique combination is a separate metric). Best practice: use structured JSON logging for easier Logs Insights queries. Set log retention to avoid accumulating costs.

# Put custom metric with dimensions
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \
  --namespace "MyApp" \
  --metric-name "OrderCount" \
  --dimensions "Environment=Production,Service=Checkout" \
  --value 42 --unit Count

# Anomaly detection alarm
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name "AnomalousCPU" \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 --statistic Average \
  --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:ops-topic

# Composite alarm (combine conditions)
aws cloudwatch put-composite-alarm --alarm-name "HighCPUOrHighLatency" \
  --alarm-rule "ALARM(HighCPU) OR ALARM(HighLatency)" \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:xxx:ops-topic

# Logs Insights (structured JSON logging)
# fields @timestamp, @message
# | filter @message like /ERROR/
# | parse @message '{"level": "*", "requestId": "*", "error": "*"}' as level, requestId, error
# | stats count() by error
# | sort @timestamp desc
# | limit 20

# Set retention policy
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/lambda/my-function --retention-in-days 30

# Dashboard
aws cloudwatch put-dashboard --dashboard-name MyDashboard --dashboard-body '{"widgets": [{"type": "metric", "x": 0, "y": 0, "width": 12, "height": 6, "properties": {"metrics": [["AWS/EC2", "CPUUtilization"]], "period": 300, "region": "us-east-1", "title": "EC2 CPU"}}]}'
